clue.text: Notes and odd bits of cash for impressionists

parts.note: two of the sol-fa notes, mi and mi

indicators.note: the odd bits are the first, third and so on, so only the odd-numbered letters of the next word count

parts.note: first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone pays street performers who do impressions with banknotes and loose change.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Notes' supplies two sol-fa notes, both mi.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimics copy other people's voices and mannerisms, which is exactly what impressionists do on stage.

clue.text: UK crime can be more sordid

indicators.note: 'can be' suggests the letters could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style remark that British crime can get seedier.
explanation.definitionFit: Muck is dirt, so muckier means dirtier, and figuratively dirty dealings are sordid ones.

clue.text: Mrs Simpson's spread

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the mother in the cartoon The Simpsons
second meaning: a short informal word for margarine

explanation.surface: It reads as asking what Mrs Simpson puts on her toast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Simpson' might suggest Wallis Simpson of the abdication; here it is the cartoon wife. The 's is read as 'is'. Marge is British slang for margarine.
explanation.definitionFit: Marge Simpson is the cartoon wife and mother, and marge is everyday British shorthand for margarine, a bread spread.

clue.text: Hired and crashed the red car

indicators.note: a crashed vehicle is wrecked and mangled, so the words after it are broken up

explanation.surface: Someone rented a red car and promptly wrote it off.
explanation.definitionFit: To charter a plane, boat or coach is to hire it for private use, so chartered is the same as hired.

clue.text: Sign with motorists in the distance

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: A driver spots a road sign with cars visible far ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC is a British breakdown and motoring club, a stock crossword stand-in for motorists.
explanation.definitionFit: A miracle is a wonder taken as a divine sign, as in the signs and wonders of scripture.

clue.text: Guy is back dealing with big house

indicators.note: going back means reading the short word from its end to its start

explanation.surface: An estate agent is back at work handling a grand property.
explanation.definitionFit: A mansion is a large, imposing residence, so 'big house' is a plain description of one.

clue.text: Lined and ordered

definitions.meaning: first meaning: marked with straight lines

explanation.surface: Paper set out neatly in lines, or an orderly arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruled paper has printed lines, and a monarch who ruled gave the orders, so both senses fit.

clue.text: B, C or D, for example, in harmony

definitions.text: B, C or D, for example
definitions.meaning: first meaning: letters that are not vowels

explanation.surface: B, C and D sound like musical notes, so the clue hints at chords in harmony.
explanation.walkthrough: B, C and D look like notes of the scale, which pairs with 'harmony'; they are really letters of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: B, C and D are non-vowel letters of the alphabet, and consonant also means agreeing or compatible.

clue.text: Say love first for selfish person

parts.note: e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
first is written 1st, read as IST

explanation.surface: Advice to put love first if you are to overcome selfishness.
explanation.walkthrough: 1st is read with the digit as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: An egoist puts self-interest above all else, which is what a selfish person does.

clue.text: Alternative script group's plant

indicators.note: alternative letters are every other one, skipping one each time

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth and so on letters

explanation.surface: It reads like a botanical classification for a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Citrus is a genus of flowering trees and shrubs, such as lemons and oranges, so it names a plant.

clue.text: Flower people follow convertible?

indicators.note: following something means coming after it in the word

parts.note: a convertible is a kind of car

explanation.surface: Crowds trailing an open-topped car, as at a parade where flowers are thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'convertible' is an example of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A carnation is a garden bloom with ruffled petals, often worn as a buttonhole.

clue.text: Particular speech from Dublin gobshite

indicators.note: taken from means the letters are lifted straight out of the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A rude Irishman's characteristic way of talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Gobshite is Irish slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is informal for jargon or a dialect, the particular vocabulary of a group or place.

clue.text: Useless patient not at treatment

indicators.note: treatment works on material and changes it, so the remaining letters are reworked
'not' tells you to leave the following short word out of the longer one

explanation.surface: A patient not attending for treatment is getting nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept describes someone clumsy or incompetent, which amounts to being no use at the task.

clue.text: Making inroads with vacant readership — they are wet!

indicators.note: making something means forming it from raw material, so the letters are rearranged
vacant means empty, so the inside of the word is cleared and just the ends remain

explanation.surface: A wet publication struggling to gain readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Raindrops are the falling droplets of rain, so of course they are wet.

clue.text: Looks at best wishes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: views or considers, as a verb
second meaning: the greeting closing a letter

explanation.surface: Glancing at the sign-off at the foot of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To regard is to gaze at something, and 'kind regards' closes a letter as a friendly greeting.

clue.text: George grades physio only 50% for science

indicators.note: only half of each word is kept, the front half in each case

explanation.surface: A teacher called George marks a physiotherapy student harshly in a science exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Geography is the academic study of the earth's landscapes and peoples, counted among the sciences.

clue.text: Fruit juice — drink for Diana?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: thick juice sold in cartons
second meaning: what the classical gods drank, Diana being a goddess

explanation.surface: Offering someone called Diana a glass of fruit juice.
explanation.walkthrough: Diana, the Roman goddess of hunting, stands for any deity, and the gods drank this.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name for thick fruit drinks and, in myth, the beverage of the Olympian deities.

clue.text: Truce for review of Erica's fee

indicators.note: a review overhauls something, so these letters are revised into a new order

parts.note: letters as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A dispute over a woman's bill settled by reviewing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceasefire is an agreed halt to fighting, the same as a truce between warring sides.

clue.text: Brilliant information about antique

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Superb details provided about an antique piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Golden can mean shining or glowing like gold, as well as excellent, so both senses match brilliant.

clue.text: Any old thing in New York is risqué

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: aught is an old word for anything at all

explanation.surface: In New York, anything goes and it is all rather racy.
explanation.definitionFit: Naughty jokes or pictures are mildly indecent, which is what risqué means.

clue.text: One leaves pie chart, creating division

indicators.note: creating means making something new from the letters left
something that leaves goes away, so the word for one is taken out

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone walks out of a meeting over a pie chart, causing a split.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapter is one of the sections a book is divided into, so it is a division of the text.

clue.text: Worms and mushrooms take note

indicators.note: to take something is to hold it within, so one word goes inside the other

explanation.surface: A gardener's list of worms and mushrooms in the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worms' looks like the garden creatures; here it means contemptible people.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a worm or a creep means they are a contemptible, slimy person, so the plurals match.

clue.text: Official employed and dismissed

parts.note: short for referee, a sports official

explanation.surface: An official who was hired and then sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss an offer or appeal is to turn it down, and refused means turned down.

clue.text: Wind giving rise to the French tears

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means reading upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: tears as in rips, not crying

explanation.surface: A gust of wind leads a French person to weep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' is the verb (rhymes with 'find'), not the breeze; 'tears' are rips, not crying.
explanation.definitionFit: To spiral is to coil or twist round and round, which is what winding means as a verb.

clue.text: What brings you down is a car up the duff

indicators.note: duff is slang for faulty or useless, so the letters are out of order

explanation.surface: The thing that depresses you is that your car has broken down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up the duff' is British slang for pregnant, so the phrase reads as one idiom; split it, and 'duff' alone signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A parachute slows a falling person so they land safely, so it is the thing that brings a skydiver down.

clue.text: Only heads can actually negotiate a lock on this?

definitions.text: Only heads can actually negotiate a lock on this?

indicators.note: heads are the tops of things, so just the opening letter of each word is used

parts.note: first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A boater wonders whether only the skilled can work the lock on this waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a lock is negotiated on a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: Canals have locks, gated chambers that raise and lower boats between water levels, which boaters must work through.

clue.text: Final decision — send off unwrapped

indicators.note: unwrapping strips the outside away, leaving only the letters inside the phrase

parts.note: everything between the first and last letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A referee's final call to send a player off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' is British slang said to close an argument: 'and that's that'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'end of' declares the matter closed, a slangy way of announcing that a decision is final.

clue.text: Costume could be red and small with snazzy top

indicators.note: 'could be' suggests the letters might be put together differently
the top of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A fancy-dress outfit described as red, small and with a flashy top.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress is a garment and, like a costume, means an outfit, as in fancy dress or national dress.

clue.text: Mature lone pirate's content in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the letters are read from right to left
the content of something is what is inside it, so the letters sit within the words

parts.note: letters running across the two words, before turning

explanation.surface: A solitary old pirate is happy in his retirement.
explanation.definitionFit: To ripen is to grow ready or fully developed, as fruit or cheese matures over time.

clue.text: Good spirits Spanish people emptied out

indicators.note: out can mean disordered, so the letters are jumbled
an emptied word has lost its middle, leaving only the outer letters

explanation.surface: Spanish people in good spirits being thrown out, perhaps from a bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in good spirits means being cheerful and contented, which is the state of happiness.

clue.text: Allegiance with kings and queens starting to switch sides

indicators.note: the opening letter moves from one side to the other, right becoming left

explanation.surface: Loyalty to the crown wavering as subjects defect.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L are standard abbreviations for right and left, the two sides.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegiance is faithful support for a ruler or cause, which is the meaning of loyalty.

clue.text: Bit of advice, as editor gave up

indicators.note: a bit of the phrase is a piece lifted out from across its words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: An editor offers a scrap of advice before quitting.
explanation.definitionFit: To cease is to stop doing something, so ceased means stopped or gave up.
